turns.prompt_text: When combining two small hives of honey bees, do you have to separate them for a little while or can you just dump one right into the other?
turns.response_html:
Don’t dump them directly; honey bees are territorial, and a "direct combine" often results in the workers attacking each other or killing the queen you intend to keep. Use the Newspaper Method to allow the colonies to acclimate to a shared scent before they physically mingle.

The Newspaper Method

This technique forces the bees to chew through a physical barrier, creating a gradual, non-aggressive transition as they intermix and establish a common pheromone profile.

  1. Prepare the Hives: Identify the queen you want to keep (or the stronger colony). Move that hive to the desired final location.
  2. Remove Inner Covers: Take the inner cover off the bottom colony.
  3. Place the Barrier: Lay a single sheet of newspaper over the top bars of the bottom hive. Use a pin or toothpick to poke 10–15 small holes in the paper; this encourages ventilation and helps them start chewing through.
  4. Stack the Hives: Place the second hive body (containing the other colony) directly on top of the newspaper.
  5. Seal It: Ensure there are no gaps where bees can escape or enter between the two boxes—everything must pass through the newspaper. Replace the hive lid on top.
  6. Wait: Over the next 24–48 hours, the bees will chew away the paper and naturally merge. You can remove the newspaper debris after 2–3 days.

Critical Considerations

  • Queen Selection: If both hives are queenright, you must find and remove the queen from the colony you are moving (the top box). If you don't, they will fight until one is killed, which risks the loss of the better queen.
  • Timing: Perform the combine in the evening when foraging has ceased and most bees are back in the hive. This minimizes drifting and confusion.
  • Frame Reorganization: If you prefer to combine them frame-by-frame instead of stacking boxes, use the Sugar Spray Method. Lightly mist both sets of bees with 1:1 sugar syrup containing a drop of lemongrass oil (or essential oil scent) to mask individual colony odors before placing them into a single box.

turns.prompt_text: I doubt I'll be able to find either Queen, so I'll probably let for them duke it out
turns.response_html:
Letting them "duke it out" is a standard, albeit slightly risky, approach, but if you go this route, you must use the Newspaper Method described previously.

Even when you intend to let the queens settle the score, do not skip the physical barrier. If you merge them without it, the worker bees from both hives will likely engage in a "balling" war—where they surround and kill one (or both) queens immediately upon contact—before the queens even have a chance to meet.

Why the Newspaper Still Matters

  • Worker Acclimation: Worker bees are the ones that actually decide which queen lives. By the time they chew through the paper, their colony odors have blended, which drastically reduces the likelihood that they will turn on either queen immediately.
  • Queen Protection: It keeps the queens separated long enough for the pheromone environment to stabilize. Once the workers are integrated, the queens will eventually encounter each other; the "survivor" is usually the younger or more vigorous queen.
  • Reduced Casualties: A direct dump often leads to mass worker mortality, which defeats the purpose of merging two small hives to build strength.

Tips for "Natural Selection"

If you are committed to letting nature take its course, you can tip the odds in favor of the queen you prefer by manipulating the hive placement:

  • Top vs. Bottom: The queen in the bottom box is statistically more likely to survive. When the bees chew through the newspaper, they move downward as a single, unified colony. Place the hive you suspect has the better queen on the bottom.
  • Frame Inspection: If you can't spot the queens, look for the brood patterns. The hive with the healthier, more uniform capped brood is likely the one with the better-performing queen. Use that box as your base.
  • Post-Merge Check: Wait about 7–10 days after the merge before opening the hive. If you inspect too early, you risk disrupting the queens during their final confrontation. After a week, look for fresh eggs; if you find them, a queen has successfully established dominance.

turns.prompt_text: Is there anything else I could do in addition to the newspaper that would help out?
turns.response_html:
To further increase the odds of a peaceful transition, focus on odor masking and resource alignment. By disrupting the unique "colony scent" of both groups simultaneously, you force them to perceive each other as part of a single, larger unit rather than as invaders.

Scent Masking Techniques

  • Essential Oil Spritz: Mix a light solution of 1:1 sugar syrup with a few drops of lemongrass oil or peppermint extract. Lightly mist the bees in both boxes right before you place the newspaper barrier. The strong, uniform scent acts as a "neutralizer," making it harder for guard bees to distinguish between the two populations.
  • Vanilla Extract: Some beekeepers prefer using pure vanilla extract (a few drops per quart of syrup). It is less pungent than essential oils but highly effective at creating a homogeneous "hive smell."
    • Warning: Do not over-saturate; you want to coat them, not soak them to the point of chilling the brood.

Strategic Adjustments

  • Swap Positions: Move both hives closer together over several days (moving them a few feet at a time) before the actual combine. If you must combine them immediately, move the "donor" hive to the location of the "receiver" hive at dusk. Foraging bees will return to the site and naturally enter the new, larger setup.
  • Provide a "Distraction": Place an entrance feeder with sugar syrup on the newly combined hive. When bees are focused on collecting food, they are significantly less defensive. The activity of feeding also keeps them occupied, giving the queens more time to move through the colony without immediate interference.
  • Reduce the Entrance: Once combined, install an entrance reducer to the smallest setting. A smaller opening is much easier for the newly integrated colony to guard against potential robbing bees while they are still sorting out their internal hierarchy.

What to Avoid

  • Don't Add Honey Frames: Avoid adding frames of honey from other hives right at the moment of combining. This can trigger a "robbing" frenzy where the bees from one box try to defend their resources against the others. Stick to the frames they already have.
  • Avoid Smoke Overload: Use just enough smoke to calm them during the physical stacking process, but do not flood the hives. Excessive smoke can mask the pheromones needed for them to identify their own nest mates, potentially causing more confusion.
